lesson.title: desde hace & Present Duration
lesson.subtitle: vivo aquí desde hace tres años — using present tense for actions that continue

hook.title: Why 'I Have Lived Here for Three Years' Is Present Tense in Spanish!
hook.content: In English, when an action began three years ago and is STILL true today, you use a past-looking form: 'I have lived here for three years'. In Spanish (just like French depuis and German seit), speakers ask: 'Are you still living here right now? Yes! Then use the PRESENT tense!' Vivo aquí desde hace tres años (word for word: 'I live here since it-makes three years')!

pattern.title: Desde (Starting Point) vs Desde Hace (Elapsed Duration)
pattern.content:
• **desde + starting point ('since')**: Vivo aquí desde enero ('I have lived here since January'), Estoy aquí desde el lunes ('I have been here since Monday').
• **desde hace + time span ('for')**: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años ('I have lived here for three years'). Never use *por or *para for ongoing duration with the present tense!
pattern.linguist_note: desde fused Latin dē + ex + dē; hace is the impersonal 3rd-person singular of hacer ('it makes [X time]').
pattern.trap_note: Never translate English 'have been here' word-for-word as *he estado aquí when you mean an unbroken state that continues right now — use simple present Estoy aquí desde...!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: for + duration (since it-makes: desde hace tres años)
I have lived here for three years (lit. I live here since it-makes 3 years)
matching_pairs.german: vivo aquí desde hace tres años

matching_pairs.english: I have been here since Monday (lit. I am here since the Monday)

exercises.target_answer: desde, desde hace, vivo aquí desde hace tres años, estoy aquí desde el lunes
exercises.meaning: since (starting point: desde enero), for + duration (since it-makes: desde hace tres años), I have lived here for three years (lit. I live here since it-makes 3 years), I have been here since Monday (lit. I am here since the Monday)
exercises.explanation: Ongoing actions that continue into the present always use the PRESENT tense + desde / desde hace.

exercises.prompt: Select every natural English rendering of 'Vivo aquí desde hace tres años':
exercises.german: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años
exercises.meaning: I have lived / have been living here for three years
renderings: I have lived here for three years
I have been living here for three years
traps: I lived here three years ago and left
I will live here in three years
exercises.target_answer: I have lived here for three years
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses the present tense (Vivo) with desde hace for any action that started in the past and is still continuing right now!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I have lived here for three years'
exercises.target_answer: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años
exercises.meaning: I have lived here for three years
exercises.explanation: Vivo (present!) + aquí + desde hace + tres años.

exercises.idea: say that you have been here since Monday
cues: I am here (present location) → Estoy aquí
exercises.meaning: I have been here since Monday
exercises.explanation: Estoy aquí desde el lunes — starting point ('Monday') uses bare desde without hace.

diagnosis.cue: Use bare desde before a calendar starting point (desde el lunes, desde enero) and desde hace before a quantity of time (desde hace tres días).

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Vivo aquí desde hace tres años'?
exercises.german: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años
exercises.natural: I have lived here for three years
options: I lived here since three years
I have lived here by three years
I have lived here for three years
I-live here since it-makes three years
exercises.target_answer: I-live here since it-makes three years
exercises.meaning: I have lived here for three years (literal Spanish blueprint: I-live here since it-makes three years)
exercises.explanation: Spanish anchors the verb in the present (Vivo) and looks back at the elapsed time with desde hace ('since it-makes').

summary.outcome: Express ongoing duration ('have been doing for X time / since Y') using the present tense with desde hace and desde.

use_example.german: Vivo en Madrid desde hace tres años y estoy aquí desde el lunes.
use_example.english: I have lived in Madrid for three years and I have been here since Monday.

summary.takeaway: If the action is still happening right now, keep the verb in the present tense and add desde (since point) or desde hace (for duration).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2001] desde vs desde hace): contrast calendar starting points with elapsed durations.

desde.context_phrase: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años.
desde.context_translation: I have lived here for three years.
desde.etymology_derivation: Just like French depuis, ongoing actions in Spanish stay in the PRESENT tense with desde hace (or hace X que + present)!

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.

estar.etymology_derivation: Latin stāre ('to stand') gives English 'stand' and 'state'. Estar describes how or where something stands right now.

año.english_meaning: year (tener X años: to be X years old)
año.context_translation: I am thirty years old (lit. I have thirty years).
año.etymology_derivation: Latin double -nn- evolved into Spanish palatal ñ (written with a tilde, originally a tiny n drawn above the first n!).

semana.context_translation: This week I have a lot of work.

lunes.etymology_derivation: Spanish uses the masculine article el/los to mean 'on [weekday]': el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays')!

tres.etymology_derivation: Shared Indo-European root with English three.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
